about: Molecules in Medical Science (MIMS) is the Part IA biochemistry and medical genetics course for Cambridge medical (and veterinary) students, hosted by the Department of Biochemistry. According to the Department's course pages (undated; consulted October 2026), lectures are built around diabetes and cancer: Michaelmas covers metabolism in health and disease, Lent the genome in health and disease and Easter the translation of biochemistry and genetics to the clinic; compulsory practicals each have a linked discussion and presentation session, and there are two compulsory PBL exercises (nutrition and metabolic disease; genetics in health and disease). In the 2023–24 exam format document (the latest that could be opened), the exam had three sections: a 1-hour MCQ paper (25% of Tripos, 50% of 2nd MB), a 2-hour data-handling (practical) paper (25% of Tripos, 50% of 2nd MB) and a 2-hour Tripos-only essay paper (50% of Tripos) with one essay from each of three subsections. Check the current MIMS Moodle page and Faculty exam information, as formats can change.

notes.h: Fuel use in the fed and fasted states, and diabetes
notes.body:
MIMS uses diabetes as a running example for Michaelmas Term because it shows what happens when the hormonal control of fuel use fails. Start with the normal picture.

Why blood glucose is controlled
- The brain depends mainly on glucose in the fed and early fasted state, and red blood cells (which lack mitochondria) rely entirely on glycolysis. Blood glucose is therefore held in a narrow range, roughly 4–7 mmol/L in health.
- Insulin, from pancreatic beta cells, is the main hormone of the fed state. Glucagon, from alpha cells, and adrenaline and cortisol oppose it.

The fed state (high insulin, low glucagon)
- Muscle and adipose tissue take up glucose through insulin-stimulated movement of GLUT4 transporters to the cell surface.
- The liver takes up glucose by GLUT2; glucokinase, which has a high Km and is not inhibited by its product, traps it as glucose 6-phosphate only when glucose is plentiful.
- Insulin promotes glycogen synthesis, glycolysis and fatty acid synthesis in the liver, triglyceride storage in adipose tissue and protein synthesis in muscle. It inhibits gluconeogenesis, glycogen breakdown and lipolysis.

The fasted state (low insulin, high glucagon)
- Early fasting: the liver releases glucose from glycogen (glycogenolysis). Muscle glycogen cannot release free glucose into the blood because muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase.
- After about a day, liver glycogen is largely used up and gluconeogenesis becomes the main glucose source. Substrates are lactate (from the Cori cycle), glycerol (from triglyceride breakdown) and amino acids such as alanine (from muscle protein). Even-chain fatty acids cannot be converted into net glucose in humans, because acetyl-CoA cannot be turned back into pyruvate.
- Lipolysis in adipose tissue releases fatty acids, which most tissues oxidise. The liver converts excess acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies (acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate; acetone forms spontaneously).
- In prolonged starvation the brain adapts to use ketone bodies for a large share of its energy, sparing muscle protein.

Diabetes mellitus
- Type 1: autoimmune destruction of beta cells leads to absolute insulin deficiency. Treated with insulin.
- Type 2: insulin resistance in liver, muscle and adipose tissue, with progressive failure of beta cells to compensate. Strongly associated with obesity and inactivity, with a substantial genetic contribution that is polygenic.
- Monogenic forms (such as maturity-onset diabetes of the young, MODY) are less common but important, because the exact gene can determine the best treatment.
- Diagnosis (WHO criteria used in the UK): fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more, 2-hour glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more in an oral glucose tolerance test or a random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more with symptoms, or HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
- With no insulin and high glucagon, the liver produces glucose and ketone bodies unchecked, while peripheral uptake of glucose falls.
- Hyperglycaemia exceeds the renal threshold, causing glycosuria and osmotic diuresis, leading to dehydration.
- Ketoacids cause a metabolic acidosis; patients breathe deeply (Kussmaul breathing) to blow off carbon dioxide.
- Insulin deficiency also lets potassium move out of cells, so total body potassium is depleted even if the blood level looks normal at first.

Exam tips: explain each metabolic change in diabetes by asking what insulin normally does in each tissue; essays often ask you to contrast the fed, fasted and diabetic states.

Proteins do most of the work in cells. Their function depends on their three-dimensional shape, which is determined by their amino acid sequence.

Levels of protein structure
- Primary: the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. The peptide bond has partial double-bond character, so it is planar and almost always trans.
- Secondary: local folding stabilised by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups. In the α-helix there are 3.6 residues per turn, with each C=O bonding to the N–H four residues along. β-sheets are formed from extended strands, either parallel or antiparallel. Proline disrupts helices.
- Tertiary: the overall fold of one chain, stabilised by the hydrophobic effect (non-polar side chains buried in the core), hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and, in extracellular proteins, disulphide bonds.
- Quaternary: the arrangement of several subunits, as in haemoglobin (two α and two β chains).
- Misfolding and aggregation underlie disease, for example amyloid deposits and the prion diseases.

Haemoglobin and allostery
- Myoglobin has a hyperbolic oxygen-binding curve; haemoglobin's curve is sigmoid because binding is cooperative. Binding at one subunit makes the others shift from the low-affinity T state towards the high-affinity R state.
- 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate binds deoxyhaemoglobin and lowers its affinity, shifting the curve to the right. Fetal haemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG less strongly and so has higher oxygen affinity, helping transfer oxygen across the placenta.
- The Bohr effect: higher CO₂ and H⁺ in active tissues lower affinity and promote unloading.
- Sickle cell disease: a single substitution of valine for glutamate at position 6 of the β-globin chain (written p.Glu7Val in modern numbering that counts the initial methionine) allows deoxygenated HbS to polymerise.

How enzymes work
- Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy; they do not change the equilibrium position or ΔG of the reaction.
- Mechanisms include binding the transition state more tightly than the substrate, acid–base catalysis, covalent catalysis and bringing substrates together in the right orientation.

Michaelis–Menten kinetics
- v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]).
- Km is the substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate; it is often used as a rough indicator of affinity (lower Km, higher apparent affinity), though strictly it depends on all the rate constants.
- kcat (turnover number) = Vmax / [total enzyme]; kcat/Km measures catalytic efficiency.
- Worked example: if Km = 2 mM, then at [S] = 2 mM, v = Vmax/2, and at [S] = 6 mM, v = 6/(2 + 6) = 0.75 Vmax.
- Lineweaver–Burk plot: 1/v against 1/[S] gives a straight line with y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km and slope Km/Vmax.

Inhibition
- Competitive: the inhibitor competes for the active site; apparent Km rises and Vmax is unchanged (overcome by high substrate). Lines cross on the y-axis.
- Non-competitive (pure): the inhibitor binds enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex equally at another site; Vmax falls and Km is unchanged.
- Uncompetitive: binds only the enzyme–substrate complex; both Vmax and Km fall (parallel lines).
- Mixed inhibition, where both change unequally, is common in practice.
- Irreversible inhibitors covalently modify the enzyme.

Regulation
- Allosteric control (for example phosphofructokinase-1), covalent modification (phosphorylation), proteolytic activation of zymogens (for example trypsinogen to trypsin) and changes in the amount of enzyme.

Exam tips: data-handling papers often give rate data; be fluent in calculating Km and Vmax from a double-reciprocal plot and in identifying inhibitor types.

Metabolism is a network of pathways that capture energy from food as ATP and reducing power, and use them to build molecules. In MIMS you are expected to know the main pathways, their key regulated steps and how they link to disease.

Free energy
- ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln([products]/[reactants]). A reaction proceeds spontaneously only if ΔG is negative. ΔG°′ is the value under standard biochemical conditions (pH 7).
- Unfavourable reactions are driven by coupling to favourable ones, most often ATP hydrolysis (ΔG°′ about −30.5 kJ/mol; the actual ΔG in cells is more negative because ATP is kept far from equilibrium).
- Reactions with large negative ΔG in cells are effectively irreversible and are usually the regulated steps.

Glycolysis (cytosol)
- Glucose → 2 pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
- Irreversible, regulated steps: hexokinase/glucokinase, phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1, the main control point) and pyruvate kinase.
- PFK-1 is activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, and inhibited by ATP and citrate. In the liver, insulin raises and glucagon lowers fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
- Without oxygen, pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.

Gluconeogenesis bypasses the three irreversible steps: pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase; fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase; glucose 6-phosphatase (liver and kidney).

Pyruvate dehydrogenase and the TCA cycle (mitochondrial matrix)
- Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and CO₂. It is irreversible and needs thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoate, CoA, FAD and NAD⁺. Thiamine deficiency impairs it.
- Each acetyl-CoA through the TCA cycle gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP (or ATP) and 2 CO₂.
- The cycle also supplies intermediates for synthesis (for example citrate for fatty acid synthesis, oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis).

Oxidative phosphorylation
- Electrons from NADH enter at complex I and from FADH₂ (via succinate dehydrogenase, complex II) at ubiquinone; they pass through complex III and cytochrome c to complex IV, which reduces oxygen to water.
- Complexes I, III and IV pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. The resulting proton-motive force drives ATP synthase: Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory (proposed 1961, Nobel Prize 1978).
- Current estimates are about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂, giving about 30–32 ATP per glucose. Older textbooks give 3 and 2, and 36–38 ATP per glucose; the exact figures are estimates and depend on the shuttle used to bring cytosolic NADH into the mitochondrion.
- Uncouplers dissipate the proton gradient as heat: UCP1 in brown fat does this physiologically; 2,4-dinitrophenol does it toxically.
- Cyanide and carbon monoxide inhibit complex IV.

Fatty acid oxidation
- Fatty acids are activated to acyl-CoA (costing the equivalent of 2 ATP) and enter mitochondria via the carnitine shuttle; carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 is inhibited by malonyl-CoA, so synthesis and oxidation do not run together.
- Worked example, palmitate (C16): 7 rounds of β-oxidation give 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH₂ and 7 NADH. Yield = 8 × 10 + 7 × 1.5 + 7 × 2.5 = 80 + 10.5 + 17.5 = 108, minus 2 for activation = 106 ATP.

Other pathways to know
- Glycogen synthesis (glycogen synthase) and breakdown (glycogen phosphorylase), reciprocally controlled by insulin and glucagon/adrenaline.
- The pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH (for fatty acid synthesis and for keeping glutathione reduced) and ribose 5-phosphate. Glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency leaves red cells vulnerable to oxidative haemolysis.

Exam tips: for each pathway, know location, inputs and outputs, regulated enzymes and the hormonal signals that switch it on or off.

Nutrition links biochemistry to everyday clinical practice. The Michaelmas problem-based learning exercise in MIMS is on nutrition and metabolic disease, so expect to apply these ideas to cases.

Energy
- Approximate energy yields: carbohydrate and protein about 17 kJ/g (4 kcal/g), fat about 37 kJ/g (9 kcal/g) and alcohol about 29 kJ/g (7 kcal/g).
- Total energy expenditure = basal metabolic rate (the largest component in most people) + the thermic effect of food + physical activity.
- Body mass index = weight (kg) / height (m)². For adults, 18.5–24.9 is the healthy range and 30 or more defines obesity; BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat and thresholds differ for some ethnic groups.

Macronutrients
- Protein: needed for nitrogen and for the nine essential amino acids that humans cannot make (histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine). Some others become conditionally essential: tyrosine, for example, must come from the diet in phenylketonuria.
- Nitrogen balance: positive in growth, pregnancy and recovery; negative in starvation, trauma and serious illness.
- Fat: a dense energy store and source of the essential fatty acids linoleic acid (omega-6) and α-linolenic acid (omega-3), which humans cannot make because they lack the desaturases to insert double bonds beyond carbon 9.
- Carbohydrate: the main fuel; dietary fibre is not digested by human enzymes but is fermented by colonic bacteria.

Micronutrients and their biochemical roles
- Thiamine (B1): thiamine pyrophosphate for pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase. Deficiency causes beriberi and, especially in alcohol misuse, Wernicke's encephalopathy.
- Riboflavin (B2): FAD and FMN. Niacin (B3): NAD⁺ and NADP⁺; deficiency causes pellagra. Pantothenate (B5): coenzyme A.
- Pyridoxine (B6): pyridoxal phosphate for transamination. Biotin: carboxylation reactions.
- Folate and vitamin B12: one-carbon metabolism and DNA synthesis. Deficiency of either causes megaloblastic anaemia; B12 deficiency also causes neurological damage. B12 absorption needs intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells.
- Vitamin C: cofactor for the hydroxylases that modify proline and lysine in collagen; deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums, poor wound healing).
- Fat-soluble vitamins: A (retinal in vision; deficiency causes night blindness), D (calcium absorption; deficiency causes rickets and osteomalacia), E (antioxidant) and K (γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X).
- Iron (haemoglobin, cytochromes) and iodine (thyroid hormones) are key minerals.

Undernutrition and refeeding
- Marasmus is severe overall energy deficiency with wasting. Kwashiorkor is characterised by oedema and fatty liver. It has traditionally been explained by protein deficiency with relatively adequate energy, but this explanation is now considered incomplete; other factors such as oxidative stress and the gut microbiome have been proposed, and the cause remains debated.
- Refeeding syndrome: when a starved patient is fed, insulin rises and drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, which can cause dangerously low blood levels. Thiamine is also used up rapidly as carbohydrate metabolism restarts.

Obesity and appetite
- Leptin, secreted by adipose tissue in proportion to fat mass, signals to the hypothalamus to reduce appetite. Rare inherited leptin deficiency causes severe early obesity, but most obese people have high leptin levels and are resistant to it.
- Obesity is a major risk factor for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and some cancers.

Exam tips: link each vitamin to the enzyme it supports, the pathway affected and the resulting clinical picture.

This topic explains how hormones such as insulin and glucagon change what cells do, linking the molecular detail back to diabetes.

Membrane structure
- Membranes are phospholipid bilayers containing cholesterol and proteins, described by the fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972). Lipids and many proteins diffuse laterally.
- Cholesterol modulates fluidity. "Lipid rafts", small ordered domains rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids, have been proposed as platforms for signalling, but their size, stability and importance in living cells are still debated.

Transport across membranes
- Simple diffusion: small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂, steroids).
- Facilitated diffusion through carriers or channels, down a concentration gradient. GLUT transporters: GLUT1 (red cells, blood–brain barrier), GLUT2 (hepatocytes, and the basolateral membranes of intestinal and kidney tubule cells; high capacity, low affinity), GLUT4 (muscle and fat; moved to the surface in response to insulin).
- Primary active transport: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP hydrolysed, maintaining gradients and membrane potential.
- Secondary active transport uses the Na⁺ gradient: SGLT1 in the gut and SGLT2 in the proximal tubule carry glucose with Na⁺. This is why oral rehydration solutions contain both glucose and salt.

Glucose-stimulated insulin secretion
- Glucose enters the beta cell and is phosphorylated by glucokinase, which acts as the glucose sensor. Rodent beta cells rely on GLUT2 for uptake, but human beta cells appear to rely mainly on GLUT1 (with GLUT3), an important species difference that is still being clarified.
- Metabolism raises the ATP/ADP ratio, which closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ (KATP) channels.
- The membrane depolarises, voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open, and Ca²⁺ entry triggers exocytosis of insulin granules.
- Sulphonylurea drugs close KATP channels directly, which is how they stimulate insulin release.

Types of receptor
- G protein-coupled receptors (seven transmembrane helices). Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP, which activates protein kinase A. Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase. Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits PIP₂ into IP₃ (releasing Ca²⁺ from the ER) and diacylglycerol (activating protein kinase C).
- Receptor tyrosine kinases: ligand binding activates the receptor's kinase domains, which phosphorylate each other and recruit signalling proteins.
- Intracellular (nuclear) receptors for lipid-soluble hormones such as steroids and thyroid hormone act as transcription factors.

Insulin and glucagon signalling
- The insulin receptor is a pre-formed dimer (α₂β₂) with tyrosine kinase activity. Insulin binding causes autophosphorylation and phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrate (IRS) proteins, which activate PI 3-kinase. The resulting PIP₃ leads to activation of Akt (protein kinase B), which promotes GLUT4 translocation and inactivates glycogen synthase kinase-3, so glycogen synthase becomes active. A separate Ras–MAP kinase branch mediates growth effects.
- Glucagon acts through a Gs-coupled receptor on hepatocytes. cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase (leading to glycogen breakdown), inactivates glycogen synthase and lowers fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (favouring gluconeogenesis).
- Adrenaline acts on several receptors: β receptors use Gs, α1 receptors use Gq and α2 receptors use Gi.

Features of signalling pathways
- Amplification: one hormone molecule can lead to many second messenger molecules and activated enzymes.
- Termination: GTP hydrolysis by the Gα subunit, phosphodiesterases breaking down cAMP, phosphatases and receptor internalisation.
- Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα, blocking its GTPase so it stays active; high cAMP in gut cells opens CFTR chloride channels, causing secretory diarrhoea.

Exam tips: be able to draw the insulin and glucagon pathways side by side, and explain how each one alters glycogen metabolism.

Lent Term in MIMS turns to the genome in health and disease. This topic covers how DNA is packaged, copied and protected.

DNA structure
- Two antiparallel polynucleotide strands form a right-handed double helix (Watson and Crick, 1953, using X-ray diffraction data from Franklin and Wilkins). A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and G with C (three).
- Strands are synthesised 5′ to 3′, and the sugar–phosphate backbone is on the outside.

The human genome
- About 3.1 billion base pairs in a haploid nuclear genome, on 23 chromosomes.
- Estimates of the number of protein-coding genes have fallen over time and now sit at roughly 19,000–20,000; exact counts differ between databases.
- Only about 1–2% of the genome codes for protein. Much of the rest is introns, regulatory sequences, non-coding RNA genes and repeated sequences (including transposable elements). How much of the non-coding genome is functional is still debated.
- The mitochondrial genome is a small circular molecule of 16,569 base pairs with 37 genes (13 proteins, 22 tRNAs and 2 rRNAs), inherited from the mother.

Chromatin
- DNA wraps about 147 base pairs around a histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4) to form a nucleosome; H1 binds linker DNA.
- Euchromatin is less condensed and generally transcriptionally active; heterochromatin is condensed and mostly silent.
- Histone modifications (acetylation, methylation) and DNA methylation influence whether genes are accessible.

DNA replication
- Semi-conservative: each daughter molecule has one old and one new strand (shown by Meselson and Stahl, 1958).
- Starts at many origins in eukaryotes. Helicase unwinds the DNA; single-strand binding proteins stabilise it; topoisomerases relieve supercoiling.
- DNA polymerases can only extend an existing primer and only in the 5′ to 3′ direction. Primase makes RNA primers.
- The leading strand is made continuously; the lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments, whose primers are removed and gaps sealed by DNA ligase.
- In eukaryotes, polymerase α–primase starts each fragment. The widely accepted model is that polymerase ε synthesises the leading strand and polymerase δ the lagging strand, though the division of labour has been debated.
- Proofreading by 3′ to 5′ exonuclease activity, plus mismatch repair, keeps the error rate extremely low.
- Telomeres: the lagging strand cannot be completed at chromosome ends. Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template, adds TTAGGG repeats. It is active in germ cells and stem cells, and reactivated in most cancers.

DNA damage and repair
- Damage arises from replication errors, spontaneous chemical change (for example deamination of cytosine to uracil, or of 5-methylcytosine to thymine, which makes CpG sites mutation hotspots), reactive oxygen species, ultraviolet light and ionising radiation.
- Mismatch repair corrects replication errors. Inherited defects in mismatch repair genes (such as MLH1 and MSH2) cause Lynch syndrome, with a high risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer.
- Base excision repair removes individual damaged bases using DNA glycosylases.
- Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. Defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancers.
- Double-strand breaks are repaired by homologous recombination (accurate, using the sister chromatid in S and G2; requires BRCA1 and BRCA2) or non-homologous end joining (works in any phase but can lose or add bases).

Exam tips: be able to explain why a specific repair defect leads to a specific cancer predisposition, and draw a replication fork with all its proteins.

notes.h: Transcription, translation and the control of gene expression
notes.body:
Gene expression turns the information in DNA into functional products, and its control explains how cells with the same genome become different.

Transcription
- Eukaryotes have three nuclear RNA polymerases: RNA polymerase I makes most rRNA, RNA polymerase II makes mRNA (and many small regulatory RNAs), and RNA polymerase III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.
- Promoters contain core elements such as the TATA box (about 25–30 bp upstream of the start site), recognised by TATA-binding protein as part of TFIID. Many promoters lack a TATA box.
- Enhancers, which may be far from the gene, bind activator proteins that recruit coactivators and the Mediator complex; DNA looping brings them to the promoter.

RNA processing
- A 5′ cap (7-methylguanosine) protects the mRNA and helps ribosome binding.
- A poly(A) tail is added at the 3′ end after cleavage.
- Introns are removed by the spliceosome (snRNPs). Introns usually begin with GU and end with AG, with a branch-point adenosine forming a lariat.
- Alternative splicing allows one gene to make several proteins. Mutations at splice sites cause disease, for example many forms of β-thalassaemia.

The genetic code and translation
- 64 codons: 61 specify amino acids and 3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). AUG codes for methionine and is the usual start codon.
- The code is degenerate (most amino acids have several codons) and almost universal. Wobble pairing at the third codon position lets one tRNA read several codons.
- Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach each amino acid to its correct tRNA, the step that actually "reads" the code.
- Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (60S and 40S subunits). The small subunit scans from the cap to the start codon. The ribosome has A (aminoacyl), P (peptidyl) and E (exit) sites. Peptide bond formation is catalysed by rRNA in the large subunit, so the ribosome is a ribozyme.
- Proteins are then folded, targeted (for example by a signal sequence to the endoplasmic reticulum) and modified (glycosylation, phosphorylation, proteolytic cleavage).

Types of mutation
- Missense (one amino acid changed), nonsense (premature stop codon, often triggering nonsense-mediated decay of the mRNA), frameshift (insertion or deletion not a multiple of three), splice-site and promoter mutations.

Control of gene expression
- Prokaryotic model: the lac operon. The lac repressor blocks transcription unless lactose (as allolactose) is present; the CAP–cAMP complex activates it when glucose is low.
- Eukaryotic control acts at every level: chromatin, transcription, RNA processing, mRNA stability, translation and protein degradation.
- Epigenetic mechanisms: DNA methylation of CpG islands in promoters silences genes; histone acetylation opens chromatin, while deacetylation closes it. These marks can be inherited through cell division without changes to the DNA sequence.
- X-inactivation: in female cells one X chromosome is silenced, coated by the non-coding RNA XIST.
- Genomic imprinting: some genes are expressed only from the maternal or paternal copy. Loss of the paternal contribution at 15q11–q13 causes Prader–Willi syndrome; loss of the maternal contribution (affecting UBE3A) causes Angelman syndrome.
- MicroRNAs bind target mRNAs and reduce their translation or stability.

Exam tips: be able to predict the effect of a given mutation on the protein, and explain imprinting disorders in terms of parent of origin.

notes.h: Cell proliferation, cell death and cancer
notes.body:
Cancer is the second running disease example in MIMS. It arises when the systems that control cell division and cell death fail because of accumulated genetic and epigenetic changes.

The cell cycle
- Phases: G1 (growth), S (DNA replication), G2 (preparation for division) and M (mitosis and cytokinesis). Non-dividing cells may sit in G0.
- Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) drive the cycle, activated by cyclins whose levels rise and fall. Cyclin D with CDK4/6 acts in G1; cyclin E with CDK2 at the G1/S transition; cyclin A in S phase; cyclin B with CDK1 at M.
- The restriction point in G1: cyclin D–CDK4/6 (then cyclin E–CDK2) phosphorylates the retinoblastoma protein (Rb), releasing E2F transcription factors that switch on S-phase genes.
- CDK inhibitors (such as p21 and p16) block progression.
- Checkpoints: the G1/S and G2/M DNA-damage checkpoints, and the spindle assembly checkpoint, which delays anaphase until all chromosomes are attached.

p53, the "guardian of the genome"
- Normally kept at low levels because MDM2 targets it for degradation.
- DNA damage stabilises p53, which activates genes including p21 (causing cell-cycle arrest for repair) and pro-apoptotic genes (such as PUMA and BAX) if the damage is severe.
- TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene across human cancers. Inherited TP53 mutations cause Li–Fraumeni syndrome.

Cell death
- Apoptosis is programmed cell death: cells shrink, chromatin condenses, the cell fragments into apoptotic bodies and it is removed by phagocytes without inflammation.
- Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway: stress shifts the balance of BCL-2 family proteins towards pro-apoptotic members (BAX, BAK), which permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane. Cytochrome c is released and binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates caspase-9.
- Extrinsic pathway: death ligands (for example Fas ligand) bind death receptors and activate caspase-8.
- Both pathways converge on executioner caspases such as caspase-3.
- Necrosis, by contrast, involves swelling, membrane rupture and inflammation.

Oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes
- Proto-oncogenes promote growth; gain-of-function mutations make them oncogenes, which act dominantly at the cellular level. Examples: point mutations in RAS (stuck in the active GTP-bound form), amplification of HER2 (ERBB2) in some breast cancers, MYC activation (for example by translocation in Burkitt lymphoma) and the BCR–ABL fusion from the t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia.
- Tumour suppressor genes restrain growth or maintain the genome; both copies usually need to be inactivated. Knudson's two-hit hypothesis (1971), based on retinoblastoma, explained why inherited cases are often bilateral and appear earlier: one hit is inherited, so only one more is needed. Examples: RB1, TP53, APC (familial adenomatous polyposis) and BRCA1/2.
- Some tumour suppressors cause disease when only one copy is lost (haploinsufficiency), so the two-hit model is not universal.

Cancer as a multistep process
- Colorectal cancer often progresses from adenoma to carcinoma as mutations accumulate, commonly in APC, then KRAS, then TP53 and others; the order is a typical pattern rather than fixed.
- The "hallmarks of cancer" framework (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2000 and 2011, further updated by Hanahan in 2022) groups the capabilities tumours acquire, such as sustained proliferative signalling, evading growth suppressors, resisting cell death, replicative immortality (telomerase), angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis, reprogrammed energy metabolism and evading immune destruction.
- Many tumours rely heavily on glycolysis even when oxygen is available (the Warburg effect). Why this happens and how it benefits the tumour are still debated.

Exam tips: distinguish oncogenes from tumour suppressors by mechanism and inheritance, and link each hallmark to a molecular example.

notes.h: Genetics and inheritance of human disease
notes.body:
The Lent PBL exercise in MIMS is on genetics in health and disease, so you should be able to draw and interpret pedigrees, calculate risks and explain the molecular basis of common inherited conditions.

Single-gene (Mendelian) inheritance
- Autosomal dominant: affected individuals in every generation, both sexes affected, male-to-male transmission possible; each child of an affected heterozygote has a 1 in 2 risk. Examples: Huntington's disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia, BRCA1/2-related cancer predisposition.
- Autosomal recessive: usually affected siblings of unaffected carrier parents; each child of two carriers has a 1 in 4 risk of being affected and 2 in 3 of unaffected siblings are carriers; consanguinity increases the risk. Examples: cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, phenylketonuria.
- X-linked recessive: mainly affects males; no male-to-male transmission; carrier mothers pass the variant to half their sons (affected) and half their daughters (carriers). Examples: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin), haemophilia A (factor VIII).
- X-linked dominant: affected fathers pass the condition to all daughters and no sons.
- Mitochondrial: maternal transmission to all children, with variable severity because of heteroplasmy (a mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA).

Complicating factors
- Reduced penetrance: not everyone with the genotype shows the condition (for example BRCA1 carriers).
- Variable expressivity: severity differs between affected people.
- New mutations: a large proportion of Duchenne cases arise without a family history.
- Anticipation: in triplet repeat disorders, repeats can expand across generations, causing earlier onset. In Huntington's disease, 40 or more CAG repeats in HTT give full penetrance and 36–39 give reduced penetrance; expansion is more likely through the father.
- Mosaicism and genomic imprinting.

Examples to know
- Cystic fibrosis: mutations in CFTR, a chloride channel; F508del is the commonest variant in UK populations. Its misfolded protein is degraded before reaching the cell surface.
- Familial hypercholesterolaemia: usually LDL receptor mutations. Heterozygous FH is more common than once thought; estimates of about 1 in 250 have replaced the older figure of 1 in 500.

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
- In a large, randomly mating population with no selection, migration or new mutation: p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
- Worked example: if cystic fibrosis affects about 1 in 2,500 births, q² = 1/2500, so q = 1/50 and p ≈ 49/50. Carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 2 × 49/50 × 1/50 ≈ 1/25.

Chromosomal disorders
- Down syndrome (trisomy 21): most cases arise from non-disjunction, usually in maternal meiosis; risk rises with maternal age. A small proportion are due to Robertsonian translocations, which can be inherited, and some are mosaic.
- Sex chromosome aneuploidies: Turner syndrome (45,X) and Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY).

Multifactorial (complex) disease
- Most common diseases, such as type 2 diabetes and coronary heart disease, depend on many genetic variants of small effect plus environment.
- The liability–threshold model: disease appears when combined liability exceeds a threshold; relatives of affected people have a higher risk, which falls with more distant relationships.
- Heritability is the proportion of variation in a trait in a particular population attributable to genetic variation; it is not a measure of how "genetic" an individual's disease is.
- Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) find variants linked to disease, but each usually explains only a small part of the risk. Polygenic risk scores combine them; their clinical usefulness is still being evaluated.

Exam tips: in pedigree questions, state the mode of inheritance with the features that support it and those that exclude alternatives; show all working in risk calculations.

notes.h: Translating biochemistry and genetics to the clinic
notes.body:
Easter Term in MIMS draws the course together by showing how biochemistry and genetics are used in diagnosis and treatment. This topic is also good preparation for the broad essay section of the Tripos paper.

Clinical biochemistry in diagnosis
- HbA1c is haemoglobin with glucose attached non-enzymatically (glycation). Because red cells live about 120 days, HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the previous two to three months. It can mislead in conditions that change red cell lifespan, such as haemolysis or some haemoglobin variants.
- The oral glucose tolerance test measures blood glucose before and two hours after a standard glucose drink.
- Enzymes and proteins released from damaged tissues are used as markers: alanine aminotransferase for liver injury and cardiac troponin for myocardial damage.
- Ketones and blood gases are measured to diagnose and monitor diabetic ketoacidosis.

Newborn screening
- In the UK a blood spot is taken from the heel at about five days of age and tested for a panel of conditions including phenylketonuria, medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD), congenital hypothyroidism, cystic fibrosis and sickle cell disease.
- PKU: deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase lets phenylalanine build up and damage the developing brain. Early diagnosis and a low-phenylalanine diet prevent intellectual disability. Women with PKU need strict control during pregnancy because high phenylalanine harms the fetus.
- MCADD: impaired fatty acid oxidation means that during fasting the patient cannot make enough ketones and becomes hypoglycaemic; preventing prolonged fasting avoids crises.

Genetic diagnosis
- Techniques include PCR-based tests for known variants, Sanger sequencing of single genes, gene panels and whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing by next-generation methods.
- England's 100,000 Genomes Project (completed in 2018) helped lead to whole-genome sequencing becoming part of NHS care through the NHS Genomic Medicine Service.
- Interpreting variants is a major challenge: many are "variants of uncertain significance". Genetic results also affect relatives, so consent, counselling and the handling of incidental findings raise ethical issues.

Genotype-guided treatment
- Monogenic diabetes: some forms of MODY caused by HNF1A variants respond well to sulphonylureas, and many babies with neonatal diabetes due to activating mutations in the KATP channel genes (KCNJ11 or ABCC8) can switch from insulin to sulphonylurea tablets, because the drug closes the overactive channel. Glucokinase (GCK) MODY causes mild, stable hyperglycaemia that usually needs no treatment. Getting the genetic diagnosis right therefore changes management.
- Pharmacogenetics: variation in drug-metabolising enzymes or immune genes can predict toxicity, for example testing TPMT activity before thiopurine drugs, or HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir.

Targeted therapies
- Imatinib inhibits the BCR–ABL tyrosine kinase in chronic myeloid leukaemia, a landmark example of a drug designed against a known molecular cause.
- Trastuzumab is an antibody against HER2 used in HER2-amplified breast cancer.
- PARP inhibitors exploit synthetic lethality: cancer cells lacking BRCA1/2 depend on alternative repair pathways, so blocking PARP kills them while sparing normal cells.
- CFTR modulators: potentiators (such as ivacaftor) increase the opening of CFTR channels that reach the surface, and correctors (such as elexacaftor and tezacaftor) help misfolded F508del protein reach the membrane. Combination therapy has transformed outcomes for many people with CF.

Gene therapy and editing
- Gene therapies are licensed for some conditions, for example spinal muscular atrophy and certain inherited retinal dystrophies.
- In 2023 the UK regulator approved a CRISPR-based therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel) for sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia; it edits patients' own blood stem cells to increase fetal haemoglobin production.
- Long-term safety, cost and fair access are ongoing questions.

Exam tips: in essays, pick a few well-understood examples and explain the molecular logic step by step, rather than listing many treatments.

cards.f: Why can't muscle glycogen raise blood glucose?
cards.b: Muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase, so glucose 6-phosphate from glycogen cannot be released as free glucose.
Lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids (e.g. alanine). Not even-chain fatty acids.

cards.f: Why can't acetyl-CoA make net glucose in humans?
cards.b: The pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is irreversible, and for every two carbons acetyl-CoA brings into the TCA cycle two are released as CO₂, so there is no net gain of oxaloacetate.
Acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate (acetone forms spontaneously), made in liver mitochondria from acetyl-CoA when fatty acid oxidation is high.
Glucokinase (liver, beta cells): high Km, not inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate, acts as a glucose sensor. Hexokinase: low Km, inhibited by product.
48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more.
Type 1: autoimmune beta-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency. Type 2: insulin resistance plus progressive beta-cell failure.

cards.f: Why is total body potassium low in DKA?
cards.b: Insulin normally drives K⁺ into cells; without it K⁺ shifts out and is lost in the osmotic diuresis, so stores fall even if plasma K⁺ is initially normal or high.
v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); Km is the [S] giving v = Vmax/2.
y-intercept = 1/Vmax; x-intercept = −1/Km; slope = Km/Vmax.

cards.f: Competitive inhibition: effect on Km and Vmax
cards.b: Apparent Km increases, Vmax unchanged; can be overcome by high [S].
Vmax decreases, Km unchanged; inhibitor binds E and ES equally at a site other than the active site.
Inhibitor binds only ES; both Vmax and apparent Km decrease (parallel Lineweaver–Burk lines).

cards.f: Net yield of glycolysis per glucose
cards.b: 2 pyruvate, 2 ATP (net) and 2 NADH.
Phosphofructokinase-1: activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate; inhibited by ATP and citrate.

cards.f: Products per acetyl-CoA in the TCA cycle
cards.b: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP (or ATP) and 2 CO₂.
About 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂ (older texts: 3 and 2); about 30–32 ATP per glucose.
Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoate, coenzyme A, FAD and NAD⁺.
Electron transport pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane; the proton-motive force drives ATP synthase (Mitchell, 1961).

cards.f: ATP yield from complete oxidation of palmitate
cards.b: 106 ATP (108 minus 2 for activation), using 2.5 per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂.

cards.f: Products of the pentose phosphate pathway
cards.b: NADPH (reductive biosynthesis, reduced glutathione) and ribose 5-phosphate (nucleotides).
Carbohydrate and protein ~17 kJ/g (4 kcal), fat ~37 kJ/g (9 kcal), alcohol ~29 kJ/g (7 kcal).
Histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine.
Linoleic acid (omega-6) and α-linolenic acid (omega-3).
Impairs pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase; causes beriberi and Wernicke's encephalopathy.

cards.f: Biochemical role of vitamin C relevant to scurvy
cards.b: Cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases that modify collagen; deficiency weakens collagen.
Needed for γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S).
On feeding after starvation, insulin drives phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ into cells, causing dangerous falls in blood levels; thiamine is rapidly consumed.
Traditionally protein deficiency with adequate energy, but this is now thought incomplete; the cause is still debated.
3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP hydrolysed.
Insulin-responsive glucose transporter of skeletal muscle and adipose tissue; stored in vesicles and moved to the surface by insulin signalling.

cards.f: How does glucose trigger insulin release?
cards.b: Glucose metabolism raises ATP/ADP, closing KATP channels; depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ entry triggers exocytosis.
Phospholipase C splits PIP₂ into IP₃ (releases ER Ca²⁺) and DAG (activates protein kinase C).
Receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylates IRS, activating PI 3-kinase; PIP₃ leads to Akt activation and GLUT4 translocation.
Gs-coupled receptor raises cAMP; PKA activates phosphorylase kinase, which activates glycogen phosphorylase.
ADP-ribosylates Gsα, inhibiting its GTPase; persistent cAMP opens CFTR in enterocytes, causing secretory diarrhoea.
Proposed cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich membrane microdomains for signalling; their existence and role in vivo remain debated.

cards.f: Size of the human haploid nuclear genome
cards.b: About 3.1 billion base pairs on 23 chromosomes.

cards.f: Approximate number of human protein-coding genes
cards.b: About 19,000–20,000; estimates vary between databases.
About 147 bp of DNA wrapped round a histone octamer (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4); H1 binds linker DNA.
Used ¹⁵N/¹⁴N density labelling to show that DNA replication is semi-conservative.
Short DNA pieces made discontinuously on the lagging strand, each started by an RNA primer and later joined by DNA ligase.
Reverse transcriptase with its own RNA template that adds TTAGGG repeats to chromosome ends; active in germ and stem cells and most cancers.
Inherited mismatch repair defect (e.g. MLH1, MSH2): high risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer.
Defective nucleotide excision repair; cannot remove UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, causing extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancers.
Pol I: most rRNA. Pol II: mRNA (and many small RNAs). Pol III: tRNA and 5S rRNA.
5′ cap, splicing of introns and 3′ polyadenylation.
UAA, UAG and UGA.
Degradation of mRNAs with a premature stop codon, reducing production of truncated proteins.
Catalytic activity forming peptide bonds; provided by rRNA in the large ribosomal subunit, so the ribosome is a ribozyme.

cards.f: Effect of DNA methylation at CpG islands
cards.b: Methylation of promoter CpG islands is associated with stable gene silencing.
Both 15q11–q13. Prader–Willi: loss of paternally expressed genes. Angelman: loss of maternal UBE3A expression.
Repressor removed by allolactose (inducer); CAP–cAMP activates transcription when glucose is low.

cards.f: Role of Rb in the cell cycle
cards.b: Unphosphorylated Rb binds and inhibits E2F; phosphorylation by cyclin D–CDK4/6 and cyclin E–CDK2 releases E2F to activate S-phase genes.

cards.f: How does p53 cause cell-cycle arrest?
cards.b: DNA damage stabilises p53, which induces p21, a CDK inhibitor, arresting cells in G1.
BAX/BAK permeabilise mitochondria; cytochrome c binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, activating caspase-9 then caspase-3.
Apoptosis: shrinkage, chromatin condensation, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation. Necrosis: swelling, rupture, inflammation.
Both alleles of a tumour suppressor must be inactivated; in inherited cases one hit is in the germline, so tumours arise earlier and are often bilateral (retinoblastoma, 1971).
t(9;22) translocation creating the BCR–ABL fusion gene encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase; chronic myeloid leukaemia.
Oncogene: gain of function, one mutant allele enough (e.g. RAS). Tumour suppressor: loss of function, usually both alleles lost (e.g. RB1, TP53).
High glycolysis with lactate production by tumours even when oxygen is available; its causes and advantages are still debated.
Affected in every generation, both sexes affected, male-to-male transmission possible; 50% risk to each child of an affected heterozygote.

cards.f: Risk to a child of two carriers of an AR disorder
cards.b: 1 in 4 affected, 1 in 2 carriers, 1 in 4 unaffected non-carriers; an unaffected sibling has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier.
Mostly affected males, transmitted through carrier females, no male-to-male transmission.
p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1; carrier frequency ≈ 2q when q is small.
q = 1/50, so carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 1/25.
Earlier onset or greater severity in successive generations, typically from expansion of unstable repeats (e.g. CAG in Huntington's disease).
A mixture of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA within a cell or person; explains variable severity of mitochondrial disease.
Proportion of variation in a trait in a population due to genetic variation; population-specific, not a measure for an individual.

cards.f: Why does HbA1c reflect 2–3 months of glycaemia?
cards.b: Glucose attaches non-enzymatically to haemoglobin over the lifetime of red cells, about 120 days.
Heel-prick sample at about day 5; screens for conditions including PKU, MCADD, congenital hypothyroidism, CF and sickle cell disease.

cards.f: Why is PKU screened for at birth?
cards.b: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency raises phenylalanine, damaging the developing brain; an early low-phenylalanine diet prevents this.
Impaired medium-chain fatty acid oxidation; on fasting, ketone production and gluconeogenesis cannot keep up, causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia.

cards.f: Why do some neonatal diabetes patients switch to sulphonylureas?
cards.b: Activating KATP channel mutations (KCNJ11/ABCC8) keep beta cells hyperpolarised; sulphonylureas close the channels so insulin is released.
Losing either of two pathways is survivable but losing both kills the cell; BRCA-deficient tumour cells die when PARP is also inhibited.
The BCR–ABL tyrosine kinase produced by the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia.
Potentiator (e.g. ivacaftor) increases channel opening; corrector (e.g. elexacaftor, tezacaftor) helps misfolded CFTR reach the cell surface.

questions.q: After three days without food, which substance is NOT a significant substrate for net glucose synthesis by the liver?
questions.why: Palmitate is an even-chain fatty acid broken down to acetyl-CoA, which cannot give net synthesis of glucose in humans. Alanine (from muscle protein), glycerol (from triglycerides) and lactate (from the Cori cycle) are all converted to glucose.

questions.q: Which change best explains the hyperglycaemia of untreated type 1 diabetes?
options: Increased hepatic glucose output together with reduced GLUT4-mediated uptake into muscle and fat
Increased glucose uptake by the brain
Excess insulin secretion causing receptor down-regulation
Loss of glucose 6-phosphatase in the liver
questions.why: Without insulin, the liver keeps making and releasing glucose while muscle and adipose tissue cannot recruit GLUT4, so glucose accumulates. Brain uptake does not rise, insulin is absent rather than in excess, and loss of liver glucose 6-phosphatase would cause hypoglycaemia (as in glycogen storage disease type I).

questions.q: Explain the biochemical basis of diabetic ketoacidosis.
markScheme: Absolute insulin deficiency with raised glucagon (and stress hormones)
Lipolysis in adipose tissue releases fatty acids to the liver
Hepatic β-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA in excess; ketogenesis makes acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate
Ketoacids cause metabolic acidosis; Kussmaul breathing compensates
Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis plus reduced peripheral uptake cause hyperglycaemia
Glycosuria and osmotic diuresis cause dehydration and electrolyte (K⁺) loss
questions.modelAnswer: DKA arises from absolute insulin deficiency with high glucagon and stress hormones. Insulin normally suppresses lipolysis, so in its absence hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue releases large amounts of fatty acids. These are taken up by the liver and oxidised, producing more acetyl-CoA than the TCA cycle can use, partly because oxaloacetate is diverted into gluconeogenesis. Liver mitochondria convert the excess into acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate, which are acids, causing a metabolic acidosis that the patient partly compensates by deep Kussmaul breathing. At the same time the liver produces glucose by gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis while muscle and fat cannot take it up, so blood glucose rises above the renal threshold. Glycosuria causes an osmotic diuresis, with dehydration and loss of potassium and other electrolytes.

questions.q: An inhibitor increases the apparent Km of an enzyme but has no effect on Vmax. What type of inhibition is this most likely to be?
questions.why: A rise in apparent Km with unchanged Vmax is the signature of competitive inhibition, overcome at high substrate. Pure non-competitive inhibition lowers Vmax without changing Km, uncompetitive inhibition lowers both, and irreversible inhibition removes active enzyme, lowering Vmax.

questions.q: Why does fetal haemoglobin have a higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin?
options: It does not show cooperative binding
It binds carbon dioxide more strongly
It contains more iron per haem
questions.why: Fetal haemoglobin (α2γ2) binds 2,3-BPG weakly, so the right shift caused by 2,3-BPG is smaller and affinity is higher. Each haem has one iron in both forms, fetal haemoglobin still binds oxygen cooperatively, and stronger CO₂ binding would lower, not raise, oxygen affinity.

questions.q: An enzyme has a Km of 4 mM and a Vmax of 120 µmol/min. Calculate the rate at 4 mM and at 12 mM substrate, and state what a competitive inhibitor would do to each value at very high substrate.
markScheme: At 4 mM: v = 120×4/(4+4) = 60 µmol/min
At 12 mM: v = 120×12/16 = 90 µmol/min
Competitive inhibitor raises apparent Km so both rates fall at these concentrations
At very high [S], rate approaches Vmax (120) with or without competitive inhibitor
questions.modelAnswer: Using v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]): at 4 mM, v = 120 × 4 / 8 = 60 µmol/min, which is Vmax/2 as expected when [S] equals Km. At 12 mM, v = 120 × 12 / 16 = 90 µmol/min, three-quarters of Vmax. A competitive inhibitor raises the apparent Km, so at both of these concentrations the rate would fall. However, because Vmax is unchanged, at very high substrate concentration the substrate outcompetes the inhibitor and the rate still approaches 120 µmol/min.

questions.q: Which of the following directly activates phosphofructokinase-1?
questions.why: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is a powerful allosteric activator of PFK-1. Citrate and high ATP inhibit it, signalling plentiful energy. Glucagon acts indirectly in the liver by lowering fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels, so it reduces rather than activates PFK-1 activity.

questions.q: Which statement about uncoupling proteins such as UCP1 is correct?
options: They allow protons to return to the matrix without making ATP, releasing energy as heat
They block electron flow at complex IV
They increase the ATP yield per NADH
questions.why: UCP1 in brown fat dissipates the proton gradient, so energy from electron transport is released as heat. Blocking complex IV is what cyanide does, uncoupling lowers rather than raises the ATP yield, and it bypasses ATP synthase instead of inhibiting it.

questions.q: Calculate the ATP yield from complete oxidation of one molecule of palmitate (C16:0), showing your working and stating your assumptions.
markScheme: Activation to palmitoyl-CoA costs 2 ATP equivalents (ATP → AMP)
7 rounds of β-oxidation: 8 acetyl-CoA, 7 FADH₂, 7 NADH
Each acetyl-CoA via TCA: 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP = 10 ATP; 8 × 10 = 80
Net 106 ATP, assuming P/O of 2.5 and 1.5
questions.modelAnswer: Palmitate is first activated to palmitoyl-CoA, which uses ATP to AMP and pyrophosphate, the equivalent of 2 ATP. Seven rounds of β-oxidation cut the 16-carbon chain into 8 acetyl-CoA, producing 7 FADH₂ and 7 NADH. Each acetyl-CoA oxidised in the TCA cycle gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP, which is 3 × 2.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 10 ATP, so 8 acetyl-CoA give 80 ATP. The 7 FADH₂ give 7 × 1.5 = 10.5 ATP and the 7 NADH give 7 × 2.5 = 17.5 ATP. The total is 108 ATP, and subtracting 2 for activation gives a net yield of 106 ATP. This assumes 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH₂; with the older values of 3 and 2 the answer would be 129.

questions.q: A patient with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with confusion, ataxia and abnormal eye movements. Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely, and which enzyme does it support?
questions.why: This is Wernicke's encephalopathy, due to thiamine deficiency; thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and other enzymes. Niacin deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia), vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, and vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding.

questions.q: Which amino acid becomes essential in the diet of a person with phenylketonuria?
questions.why: Tyrosine is normally made from phenylalanine by phenylalanine hydroxylase, which is defective in PKU, so tyrosine must come from the diet. Phenylalanine is always essential and must be restricted in PKU, and alanine and glutamine can be made from other precursors.

questions.q: Explain the biochemical basis of refeeding syndrome and why it is a risk in patients who have been starved.
markScheme: During starvation, insulin low, fat and ketones used; intracellular phosphate, K⁺, Mg²⁺ depleted though plasma levels may be normal
Feeding carbohydrate raises insulin
Insulin drives glucose, phosphate, K⁺ and Mg²⁺ into cells; phosphate used to make phosphorylated intermediates and ATP
Falls in plasma phosphate, K⁺, Mg²⁺ cause arrhythmias, weakness, respiratory and cardiac failure
Thiamine consumed as carbohydrate metabolism resumes; deficiency can precipitate Wernicke's
questions.modelAnswer: During prolonged starvation insulin is low and the body runs mainly on fat and ketones. Total body stores of phosphate, potassium and magnesium fall, although blood levels may stay near normal because they are drawn from cells. When feeding restarts, especially with carbohydrate, insulin secretion rises sharply. Insulin drives glucose into cells along with phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and phosphate is consumed in making phosphorylated glycolytic intermediates and ATP. Blood levels of these ions can therefore fall abruptly, causing muscle weakness, cardiac arrhythmias and heart and respiratory failure. Thiamine, needed for carbohydrate metabolism, is also used up quickly, and its deficiency can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy. Feeding is therefore restarted cautiously with monitoring and replacement of electrolytes and thiamine.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes glucose-stimulated insulin secretion?
options: Glucose binds a GPCR, cAMP falls and K⁺ channels open
Glucose enters by SGLT2, Na⁺ entry depolarises the cell directly
ATP falls, KATP channels open and Ca²⁺ is released from mitochondria
Glucose metabolism raises ATP, KATP channels close, the cell depolarises and Ca²⁺ enters
questions.why: Rising ATP closes KATP channels, depolarising the membrane so voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open and insulin granules fuse. Glucose is not sensed through a GPCR, and beta cells do not take it up by SGLT2 (a kidney tubule transporter) or depolarise through Na⁺ co-transport, and falling ATP would open KATP channels and hyperpolarise the cell, stopping secretion.

questions.q: A drug that inhibits cAMP phosphodiesterase in hepatocytes would be expected to:
options: Prolong the effects of glucagon on glycogen breakdown
Mimic the effects of insulin on GLUT4
Block the action of glucagon at its receptor
questions.why: Phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP, so inhibiting it keeps cAMP high and prolongs PKA-mediated glycogenolysis triggered by glucagon. It does not act like insulin, it does not block the glucagon receptor, and higher cAMP activates rather than inhibits PKA.

questions.q: Compare the mechanisms by which insulin and glucagon regulate glycogen metabolism in the liver.
markScheme: Glucagon: Gs-coupled GPCR → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA
PKA activates phosphorylase kinase → glycogen phosphorylase active; PKA inactivates glycogen synthase
Insulin: receptor tyrosine kinase → IRS → PI3K → Akt
Akt inhibits GSK3 → glycogen synthase dephosphorylated/active; insulin also activates phosphatases and lowers cAMP (phosphodiesterase)
Net reciprocal control: phosphorylation favours breakdown, dephosphorylation favours synthesis
questions.modelAnswer: Glucagon binds a Gs-coupled receptor on hepatocytes, activating adenylyl cyclase and raising cAMP, which activates protein kinase A. PKA phosphorylates and activates phosphorylase kinase, which in turn phosphorylates and activates glycogen phosphorylase, so glycogen is broken down. PKA also phosphorylates glycogen synthase, inactivating it. Insulin binds its receptor tyrosine kinase, which phosphorylates IRS proteins and activates PI 3-kinase and then Akt. Akt phosphorylates and inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3, so glycogen synthase is less phosphorylated and becomes active; insulin also promotes protein phosphatase activity and lowers cAMP by activating phosphodiesterase. Overall the two hormones act reciprocally: phosphorylation driven by glucagon favours breakdown, while dephosphorylation promoted by insulin favours synthesis.

questions.q: Which DNA repair pathway depends on BRCA1 and BRCA2?
options: Homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks
Nucleotide excision repair of pyrimidine dimers
questions.why: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are needed for homologous recombination, which repairs double-strand breaks accurately using the sister chromatid. Nucleotide excision repair is defective in xeroderma pigmentosum, mismatch repair in Lynch syndrome, and base excision repair uses DNA glycosylases.

questions.q: Why are CpG dinucleotides mutation hotspots in the human genome?
options: CpG sites are always in introns
Guanine is unstable at CpG sites
Methylated cytosine can deaminate to thymine, which is not recognised as foreign
CpG sites cannot be replicated by polymerase δ
questions.why: 5-Methylcytosine deaminates to thymine, a normal DNA base, so the resulting G–T mismatch is not always repaired correctly, producing C to T transitions. Replication of CpG sites is normal, many CpG sites (including CpG islands) lie in promoters and exons, and guanine is not especially unstable there.

questions.q: Explain why DNA replication requires both continuous and discontinuous synthesis, and outline how the lagging strand is completed.
markScheme: Strands antiparallel; DNA polymerase only synthesises 5′→3′ and needs a primer
Leading strand made continuously towards the fork
Lagging strand made in Okazaki fragments away from the fork
Primase lays down RNA primers; polymerase extends; primers removed and replaced with DNA
DNA ligase seals the nicks; end-replication problem solved by telomerase
questions.modelAnswer: The two strands of DNA are antiparallel, but DNA polymerases can only add nucleotides to the 3′ end of an existing primer, synthesising 5′ to 3′. At a replication fork one template allows synthesis in the same direction as fork movement, so the leading strand is made continuously. The other template runs the opposite way, so the lagging strand has to be made in short Okazaki fragments, each started at a new RNA primer laid down by primase and extended away from the fork. The RNA primers are later removed and replaced by DNA, and DNA ligase seals the remaining nicks. Because the final primer at the very end of a chromosome cannot be replaced, chromosomes would shorten each cycle; telomerase counters this in germ and stem cells by adding telomeric repeats.

questions.q: A single-base insertion occurs in the middle of an exon. What is the most likely effect?
options: A single amino acid substitution only
No effect because the code is degenerate
A frameshift altering all downstream codons, often creating a premature stop codon
questions.why: Inserting one base shifts the reading frame, changing every downstream codon and usually producing a premature stop codon. A single substitution would be a missense change, degeneracy only protects some substitutions at the third position, and a coding insertion does not affect capping.

questions.q: A child has a deletion of 15q11–q13 on the chromosome inherited from the father. Which condition is expected?
questions.why: Genes in this region that are expressed only from the paternal copy are lost, causing Prader–Willi syndrome. A maternal deletion would cause Angelman syndrome. Turner syndrome is 45,X and fragile X is a CGG repeat expansion in FMR1.

questions.q: Describe how a eukaryotic protein-coding gene is transcribed and its RNA processed before export from the nucleus.
markScheme: Activators bind enhancers; general transcription factors (TFIID/TBP at TATA) assemble at the promoter with RNA polymerase II
Chromatin opened by histone acetylation/remodelling
5′ 7-methylguanosine cap added early
Introns removed by spliceosome (GU…AG, branch-point A, lariat); alternative splicing possible
3′ cleavage and poly(A) tail; mature mRNA exported through nuclear pores
questions.modelAnswer: Transcription begins when activator proteins bind enhancers and recruit coactivators and chromatin-modifying enzymes, such as histone acetyltransferases, which open the chromatin. General transcription factors assemble at the core promoter, with TATA-binding protein in TFIID recognising the TATA box where present, and recruit RNA polymerase II. As soon as transcription begins, a 7-methylguanosine cap is added to the 5′ end. Introns are removed by the spliceosome, which recognises the GU at the 5′ splice site, the AG at the 3′ end and a branch-point adenosine that forms a lariat; alternative splicing can produce different mRNAs from one gene. The transcript is cleaved at the 3′ end and a poly(A) tail is added. The mature mRNA, bound by export proteins, then leaves through nuclear pores for translation.

questions.q: A mutation in RAS that prevents hydrolysis of bound GTP would be expected to:
options: Keep RAS active, driving proliferation as an oncogene
Inactivate RAS, acting as a loss-of-function tumour suppressor mutation
questions.why: RAS is active when GTP is bound, so loss of GTPase activity locks it on and continuously signals growth, a classic gain-of-function oncogenic mutation. It does not inactivate RAS, and it does not directly trigger the extrinsic apoptotic pathway or stabilise p53.

questions.q: Why do children with inherited retinoblastoma often develop tumours in both eyes?
options: Both RB1 alleles are inherited in mutant form
Every retinal cell already carries one inactivated RB1 allele, so only one further somatic hit is needed
The inherited mutation is an activating oncogene mutation
questions.why: In hereditary cases the first hit is in the germline, so a single somatic event in any of many retinal cells completes inactivation, making bilateral and earlier tumours likely. RB1 is a tumour suppressor, not an oncogene; affected children usually inherit only one mutant allele; and retinal cells can undergo apoptosis.

questions.q: Explain how p53 and Rb normally prevent uncontrolled cell proliferation, and what happens when they are lost.
markScheme: Rb binds E2F in G1, blocking S-phase gene transcription
Phosphorylation by cyclin D–CDK4/6 and cyclin E–CDK2 releases E2F at the restriction point
p53 stabilised by DNA damage (escapes MDM2), induces p21 (arrest) and pro-apoptotic genes
Loss of Rb: E2F free, uncontrolled entry into S phase
Loss of p53: damaged cells continue to divide and avoid apoptosis, causing genomic instability
Both are tumour suppressors; two hits usually needed (retinoblastoma; Li–Fraumeni)
questions.modelAnswer: Rb controls entry into S phase. In early G1, unphosphorylated Rb binds E2F transcription factors and prevents them switching on genes needed for DNA replication. When growth signals raise cyclin D, cyclin D–CDK4/6 and then cyclin E–CDK2 phosphorylate Rb, releasing E2F so the cell passes the restriction point. p53 responds to DNA damage and other stresses. It is normally degraded through MDM2, but damage stabilises it, and p53 then activates transcription of p21, a CDK inhibitor that halts the cycle to allow repair, and of pro-apoptotic genes such as PUMA and BAX if damage is beyond repair. If Rb is lost, E2F is permanently free and cells enter S phase without proper growth signals. If p53 is lost, cells with damaged DNA keep dividing and avoid apoptosis, so mutations accumulate and the genome becomes unstable. Both are tumour suppressors, usually requiring loss of both alleles; inherited mutations cause retinoblastoma and Li–Fraumeni syndrome respectively.

questions.q: A man with haemophilia A has children with a woman who is not a carrier. What is the expected outcome?
options: All daughters are carriers and no sons are affected
questions.why: A father passes his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y to every son, so all daughters are obligate carriers and sons, who receive their mother's normal X, are unaffected. Half of sons being affected would need a carrier mother, since sons get their X from her. Not all children are affected: daughters get a normal X from the mother and sons get no X from the father. Half of daughters being carriers is the pattern for a carrier mother with an unaffected father; here every daughter inherits the father's affected X.

questions.q: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, an autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 10,000 births. What is the approximate carrier frequency?
questions.why: q² = 1/10,000, so q = 1/100 and the carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 2 × 1/100 = 1/50. 1 in 100 is the allele frequency q, not the carrier frequency; 1 in 25 is the carrier frequency for an incidence of about 1 in 2,500 (q = 1/50); and 1 in 5,000 comes from doubling the disease frequency q² instead of the allele frequency q.

questions.q: Cystic fibrosis affects about 1 in 2,500 births in a population. A healthy woman whose brother has cystic fibrosis has a partner from the general population with no family history. Calculate the risk that their first child will have cystic fibrosis, showing your working.
markScheme: Woman's parents are both carriers; as she is unaffected, her carrier risk is 2/3
Population: q² = 1/2500, q = 1/50, carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 1/25
Risk both carriers × 1/4 for an affected child
States Hardy–Weinberg assumptions (random mating, no selection etc.)
questions.modelAnswer: The woman's brother is affected, so both her parents are carriers. Of their unaffected children, two-thirds are carriers, so the woman's carrier risk is 2/3. For her partner, use Hardy–Weinberg: q² = 1/2,500, so q = 1/50, and the carrier frequency 2pq is approximately 2 × 1/50 = 1/25. If both are carriers, each child has a 1/4 chance of being affected. The risk for their first child is therefore 2/3 × 1/25 × 1/4 = 2/300 = 1/150. This assumes the population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium and ignores carrier testing, which in practice would be offered to refine the risk.

questions.q: Why can PARP inhibitors selectively kill tumour cells with loss of BRCA1 or BRCA2?
options: BRCA-deficient cells cannot replicate DNA at all
The tumour cells lack homologous recombination and depend on PARP-mediated repair, so blocking both pathways is lethal
PARP inhibitors directly restore BRCA function
PARP is only expressed in tumour cells
questions.why: This is synthetic lethality: normal cells can repair damage by homologous recombination, but BRCA-deficient cells cannot and rely on PARP-dependent pathways, so inhibition leaves them unable to cope. PARP inhibitors do not restore BRCA, PARP is present in normal cells too, and BRCA-deficient cells do replicate DNA.

questions.q: A baby is diagnosed with permanent neonatal diabetes caused by an activating mutation in KCNJ11. Why might sulphonylurea tablets work instead of insulin?
options: They increase GLUT4 expression in muscle
They close the overactive KATP channels, allowing beta-cell depolarisation and insulin release
They replace insulin at its receptor
questions.why: The mutation keeps KATP channels open, so beta cells stay hyperpolarised and do not secrete insulin; sulphonylureas bind the channel complex and close it, restoring secretion. They are not insulin analogues, their main action is not on GLUT4 expression, and blocking glucagon alone would not correct insulin deficiency.

questions.q: Using one example, explain how understanding the molecular basis of an inherited disease has led to a targeted treatment.
markScheme: Names disease and gene/protein (e.g. CF and CFTR chloride channel)
Explains molecular defect (e.g. F508del misfolding and degradation; gating mutations reduce opening)
Explains how the treatment targets the defect (correctors aid folding/trafficking; potentiators increase opening)
Notes genotype-dependence: treatment chosen according to variant
Notes outcomes/limitations (improved lung function; not all variants respond; cost and access)
questions.modelAnswer: Cystic fibrosis is caused by variants in CFTR, which encodes a chloride channel in epithelial cells. Loss of channel function leads to thick, dehydrated secretions in the lungs, pancreas and other organs. Different variants cause different molecular defects: F508del, the commonest in the UK, causes the protein to misfold so that most is degraded before reaching the cell surface, whereas gating variants such as G551D produce channels that reach the membrane but rarely open. Understanding this led to CFTR modulators. Potentiators such as ivacaftor increase the probability that channels at the surface open, which is effective for gating variants. Correctors such as elexacaftor and tezacaftor help F508del protein fold and traffic to the membrane, and combined with a potentiator they restore substantial function. Because treatment depends on the specific variant, genotyping guides prescribing. The therapy improves lung function and quality of life, but a minority of variants do not respond, and long-term effects and cost remain issues.

questions.q: Compare the metabolic changes in the liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue in prolonged fasting with those in untreated type 1 diabetes mellitus, and explain why only the diabetic state commonly leads to ketoacidosis.
markScheme: Hormonal context: fasting low insulin/high glucagon but some insulin present; type 1 diabetes absolute insulin deficiency
Liver: glycogenolysis then gluconeogenesis; ketogenesis from fatty acid oxidation in both states
Muscle: fatty acid and ketone oxidation in fasting, proteolysis supplies alanine; in diabetes no GLUT4 uptake and increased proteolysis
Adipose: controlled lipolysis in fasting; unrestrained lipolysis in diabetes
Fasting: ketones rise moderately and brain adapts to use them; residual insulin limits lipolysis and ketogenesis
Diabetes: hyperglycaemia, glycosuria, osmotic diuresis; unchecked ketogenesis exceeds use and buffering → acidosis
Molecular mechanisms (insulin/glucagon signalling, GLUT4, PKA, malonyl-CoA/CPT1)
Clear comparative structure and accurate biochemistry
questions.modelAnswer:
Both prolonged fasting and untreated type 1 diabetes are states of low insulin action and high counter-regulatory hormones, and both shift the body towards using fat. The crucial difference is that in fasting a small amount of insulin is still secreted and blood glucose is low or normal, whereas in type 1 diabetes insulin is absent.

Liver. In early fasting glucagon, acting through a Gs-coupled receptor, cAMP and protein kinase A, activates glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthase, releasing glucose. After about a day glycogen is depleted and gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids dominates, aided by low fructose 2,6-bisphosphate. Fatty acids from adipose tissue are oxidised: low insulin and high glucagon reduce acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity, malonyl-CoA falls and carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 is released from inhibition. Excess acetyl-CoA is converted to ketone bodies. In type 1 diabetes the same pathways run, but without any restraint: gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis continue despite high blood glucose, and the flood of fatty acids drives very high rates of ketogenesis.

Skeletal muscle. In fasting, muscle oxidises fatty acids and ketones, sparing glucose for the brain and red cells, and releases amino acids, particularly alanine and glutamine, for gluconeogenesis. As fasting is prolonged and the brain uses more ketones, protein breakdown slows. In type 1 diabetes the lack of insulin prevents GLUT4 translocation, so glucose uptake falls despite hyperglycaemia, and protein breakdown is excessive, contributing to wasting.

Adipose tissue. In fasting, low insulin allows hormone-sensitive lipase to release fatty acids and glycerol, but the small amount of insulin present restrains lipolysis. In type 1 diabetes, with no insulin, lipolysis is unrestrained and fatty acid release is very high.

Why ketoacidosis occurs in diabetes. In prolonged fasting, blood ketones rise to a level that the brain and muscle can use, and ketones themselves stimulate a little insulin secretion, which limits further lipolysis. The result is ketosis without dangerous acidosis. In type 1 diabetes this negative feedback is absent. Ketone production far exceeds use, and the ketoacids overwhelm bicarbonate buffering, producing metabolic acidosis. At the same time hyperglycaemia exceeds the renal threshold, causing glycosuria and osmotic diuresis, which leads to dehydration, reduced kidney function and further accumulation of acids, while potassium is lost from cells and in urine. Kussmaul breathing partly compensates.

In summary, fasting is a regulated adaptation in which residual insulin keeps fat breakdown proportional to need, while untreated type 1 diabetes removes this brake, turning a useful adaptation into a life-threatening metabolic emergency.

questions.q:
Data handling. The initial rate (v, µmol/min) of an enzyme was measured at different substrate concentrations ([S], mM), without inhibitor and in the presence of 1 mM of compound X.
[S] = 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 mM
No inhibitor: v = 20.0, 33.3, 50.0, 66.7, 80.0
With 1 mM X: v = 7.7, 14.3, 25.0, 40.0, 57.1
(a) Construct a double-reciprocal (Lineweaver–Burk) table and determine Km and Vmax without inhibitor. (6 marks)
(b) Determine the apparent Km and Vmax with X, and identify the type of inhibition. (6 marks)
(c) Calculate the inhibition constant Ki of X. (4 marks)
(d) Give one limitation of the double-reciprocal plot and one alternative approach. (4 marks)
markScheme: (a) Intercept 0.010 → Vmax = 100 µmol/min; slope 0.020 → Km = 0.020 × 100 = 2 mM (x-intercept −0.5)
(b) 1/v with X: 0.130, 0.070, 0.040, 0.025, 0.0175; intercept 0.010 → Vmax unchanged at 100
(b) Slope 0.060 → apparent Km = 6 mM; lines meet on y-axis → competitive inhibition
(d) Reciprocal plot gives most weight to least accurate low-[S] points; alternatives: non-linear regression to Michaelis–Menten equation (or Eadie–Hofstee/Hanes plots)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Take reciprocals. 1/[S] (mM⁻¹) = 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125. Without inhibitor, 1/v (min/µmol) = 1/20.0 = 0.050, 1/33.3 = 0.030, 1/50.0 = 0.020, 1/66.7 = 0.015 and 1/80.0 = 0.0125.
These points lie on a straight line. The slope between the first and last points is (0.050 − 0.0125)/(2 − 0.125) = 0.0375/1.875 = 0.020 min·mM/µmol. The y-intercept is 0.050 − 0.020 × 2 = 0.010 min/µmol.
Vmax = 1/0.010 = 100 µmol/min. Slope = Km/Vmax, so Km = 0.020 × 100 = 2 mM. Check: the x-intercept is −0.010/0.020 = −0.5 mM⁻¹ = −1/Km, so Km = 2 mM. At [S] = 2 mM, v = 50, half of Vmax, as expected.

(b) With 1 mM X, 1/v = 1/7.7 = 0.130, 1/14.3 = 0.070, 1/25.0 = 0.040, 1/40.0 = 0.025 and 1/57.1 = 0.0175.
Slope = (0.130 − 0.0175)/(2 − 0.125) = 0.1125/1.875 = 0.060. Intercept = 0.130 − 0.060 × 2 = 0.010, so Vmax is still 100 µmol/min. Apparent Km = slope × Vmax = 0.060 × 100 = 6 mM.
Because Vmax is unchanged and the apparent Km has increased, the two lines meet on the y-axis: X is a competitive inhibitor. It most likely binds the active site, and its effect can be overcome by high substrate concentration.

(c) For competitive inhibition, apparent Km = Km(1 + [I]/Ki). So 6 = 2(1 + 1/Ki), giving 1 + 1/Ki = 3, 1/Ki = 2 mM⁻¹, and Ki = 0.5 mM.

(d) The double-reciprocal transformation distorts experimental error: the points at the lowest substrate concentrations, where rates are smallest and least precise, have the largest values of 1/[S] and 1/v and so exert the most influence on the fitted line. A better approach is to fit the untransformed data directly to the Michaelis–Menten equation by non-linear regression, which weights the points more appropriately. Alternative linear plots, such as the Hanes–Woolf plot ([S]/v against [S]), spread the error more evenly than the Lineweaver–Burk plot.
